summary: Presents the High-level Entity Management Protocol (HEMP), the application protocol used by HEMS to manage network entities such as hosts, gateways and front-end machines. It assumes the reader knows ASN.1 and the system described in RFC 1021.

eli5.summary: If HEMS is a remote control, this is the language the buttons use to talk to the machine being controlled.

questions: how does hems talk to network devices
subtitle: The message envelope HEMS uses to monitor and control hosts, gateways and other network entities.

tldr.problem: Managing hosts, gateways and front-end machines from afar needs a common way to wrap every request and reply, check who sent it, and keep sensitive data private.
tldr.mechanism: HEMP wraps each message in an ASN.1 envelope with optional encryption, reply encryption and authentication sections, then a common header and an application-specific data section. It runs over TCP for request-response and UDP for events.
tldr.outcome: The memo defines the envelope and the protocol error messages only. No encryption types are assigned, and the contents of the data section are left to the applications.

sections.title: What HEMP Is and How It Is Used
sections.content:
The High-Level Entity Management Protocol (HEMP) is an application protocol for managing network entities such as hosts, gateways and front-end machines. It is one component of the High-Level Entity Management System (HEMS) described in RFC 1021, and it relies on existing transport protocols to carry its messages.

The authors name three essential features of a management protocol: a standard encapsulation scheme for all interactions, an authentication facility that can verify messages and limit access, and the ability to encrypt messages to protect sensitive information. HEMP is meant for both monitoring and control.

A message is an arbitrarily long sequence of octets. Five types are defined: request, reply, event, protocol error and application error. Reply, protocol error and application error messages are sent only in reaction to a request, and are called responses.

An application sends a request to an entity and normally gets one response: a reply if the request was valid, or an error message if it was not (for example, if authentication failed). Protocol errors come from problems with the HEMP encapsulation itself; anything that goes wrong while processing the contents is an application error. Because the entity may already be sending a reply when it finds such a problem, an application error may show up inside the reply instead of as a separate message.

Entities are not required to send error messages, since on secure networks returning them may be undesirable. They are encouraged on friendly networks.

Event messages are unsolicited notices from an entity to an address expected to correspond to one or more management centers, possibly a multicast address. They typically report important state changes, such as an interface going down or the entity running out of network buffers.
sections.eli5: You can ask a machine a question and get an answer back, or the machine can shout on its own when something goes wrong, like a smoke alarm.

sections.title: The Standard Message Format
sections.content:
Every HEMP message has the same general form, written in ASN.1: a leader (the ASN.1 tag and message length), then an optional encryption section, an optional reply encryption section, an optional authentication section, a mandatory common header and a data section. The four sections after the leader are also ASN.1 encoded.

The order matters. The encryption section comes first so everything after it, which may be sensitive, can be encrypted. The authentication section comes before the header so that a message failing authentication can be discarded without any header processing.

The common header holds the link (which version of HEMS is in use), the messageType (request 0, reply 1, event 2, protocol error 3, application error 4), a messageId and a resourceId. The messageId is set in a request and echoed in the response so the application can match them up; applications should avoid reusing one for a substantial time, even across machine crashes. For events, the messageId counts event messages so lost ones can be detected; it resets to 0 on each reboot, and by convention event 0 is a reboot event. The resourceId exists for ISO compatibility and matches the resource ID used by the Common Management Information Protocol.

The data section is application specific, and outside this memo except for protocol error messages.
sections.eli5: Each message is like a letter with layers: a lock, a password, a label with a number, and then the real note inside. The password check comes early so a fake letter gets thrown out fast.

sections.title: Encryption and Reply Encryption
sections.content:
Monitoring data can be sensitive. A traffic matrix, for example, can reveal communication patterns in an organization. Access control stops unauthorized people from asking, but only encryption stops eavesdroppers. The RFC notes that HEMP encryption does not protect against traffic analysis, and suggests link-level encryption for organizations concerned about that.

The encryption section carries an encryptType number and encryptData (for example a key). If it is omitted, no decryption is needed. If present, data is encrypted starting with the first octet after the section.

The reply encryption section lets the requester ask for the reply to be encrypted even if the request was not, or with a different key or scheme, as with a public key system. If omitted, the reply uses the method in the encryption section. If an entity does not support the requested method it may send no reply, or, at the implementor's discretion, a protocol error. The RFC states that currently no encryption types are assigned.
sections.eli5: You can tell the machine to lock its answer with a special key so nobody on the way can read it. The memo leaves the actual lock types for later.

sections.title: Authentication
sections.content:
Authentication lets a receiver confirm that a message really came from the claimed entity, or that the sender is allowed to ask. The RFC gives two reasons: trusting an event such as an unstable trunk link before re-routing traffic, and limiting requests to authorized applications, since requests cost an entity processing time.

The authentication section has an authenticateType and authenticateData. If it is omitted, the message is not authenticated. Two types are defined: password(1), where the data is an octet string of any length compared against a password assigned to the entity, and encryption(2), which only states that the encryption method already authenticates the message (the receiver should confirm that it does). The RFC calls the password scheme slightly more powerful than the password scheme then used for monitoring on the Internet.

A message that fails authentication should be discarded. If the type is unknown or the section is missing, the implementation may discard or process it, but requests with unknown authentication types should be logged as potential intrusions and not processed.
sections.eli5: The password part is like a knock at the door: the machine only listens if you give the right knock. If the knock is wrong, it ignores you.

sections.title: Protocol Error Messages
sections.content:
Protocol error messages are the one case where this memo defines the data section. It holds a protoErrorCode, a protoErrorOffset (the number of the octet where the error was found, counting the first octet as 0) and a protoErrorDescribed string. The format matches the language processing error format in RFC 1024, with codes chosen so they do not overlap.

The message for code 3 is defined for completeness, but implementations are strongly discouraged from sending it, since reporting authentication failures may help intruders. The RFC recommends logging them as possible security problems instead. A wrong version number (code 2) may also signal intrusion and should be logged at security-conscious sites. For code 5, the entity could not read the common header, so the messageId in the error is set to 0.
sections.eli5: If a message is garbled, the machine can send back a note saying what went wrong and where. It stays quiet about wrong passwords so burglars learn nothing.

sections.title: Transport Protocols
sections.content:
The authors say there was considerable debate about the right transport. Request-response exchanges can move arbitrary amounts of data in both directions and are believed to need reliable transport. Events are small and need not be delivered reliably. Opinion leaned toward a transaction protocol (see RFC 955), but the community was still experimenting.

So the memo defines two transports for near-term use: TCP for all request-response interactions and UDP for event messages. Using UDP for request-response is strongly discouraged. Forward-looking groups are encouraged to use a transaction protocol, and experiments with the Versatile Message Transaction Protocol (VMTP) were planned.
sections.eli5: Questions and answers go by the careful delivery service, because they can be big. Quick alarm shouts go by the fast, no-promises service.

layers.label: Encryption section
layers.detail: Optional; what the receiver needs to decrypt

layers.label: Reply encryption section
layers.detail: Optional; how to encrypt the reply

layers.label: Authentication section
layers.detail: Optional; lets the receiver authenticate the message

items.label: ASN.1 format error
items.desc: Error in parsing the message, such as an unknown type or invalid ASN.1 syntax.

items.label: Wrong HEMP version
items.desc: Version number in the common header is invalid; possible intrusion.

items.label: Authentication error
items.desc: Authentication failed; sending it is strongly discouraged.

items.label: ReplyEncryption not supported
items.desc: The entity does not support the requested reply encryption.

items.label: Decryption failed
items.desc: The entity could not decrypt the message; messageId is set to 0.

items.label: Application failed
items.desc: An application failure made it impossible to process the message.
